items.evidenceSummary:
Sudden shifts in sleep and wake times disrupt the body’s circadian rhythm, leading to negative effects on cognitive function, metabolism, and overall health. Research indicates that irregular sleep patterns can cause circadian misalignment, increasing the risk of obesity, diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and mood disorders[97]. The body's internal clock relies on consistent light exposure and melatonin secretion to regulate sleep-wake cycles, and erratic sleep schedules interfere with these natural processes, resulting in poor sleep quality, daytime fatigue, and impaired focus[11].

Health organizations, including the American Academy of Sleep Medicine and the National Sleep Foundation, emphasize the importance of maintaining a stable sleep schedule [6],[98]. Keeping a consistent sleep-wake cycle supports brain function, hormone regulation, and physical performance while reducing the risks associated with chronic sleep deprivation and metabolic dysfunction.

items.evidenceSummary: Studies indicate that maintaining an optimal sleep temperature, typically between 60–67°F (16–19°C), can enhance sleep quality by supporting the body's natural thermoregulation process[45][46]. As bedtime approaches, the body's core temperature naturally drops, signaling that it's time to sleep. A cooler room helps facilitate this process, making it easier to fall asleep and stay asleep. Conversely, a room that is too warm can cause discomfort, increased wakefulness, and disruptions in deep sleep stages, leading to a less restorative sleep experience.

items.plain: Block light from windows with heavy curtains or an eye mask.

items.category: Sleep Hygiene (General Behavioral and Environmental Factors)
items.evidenceSummary:
Light exposure plays a crucial role in regulating the body’s circadian rhythm, which controls sleep-wake cycles. Studies show that even small amounts of artificial light at night can disrupt melatonin production, leading to difficulty falling asleep, frequent awakenings, and reduced sleep quality. Exposure to streetlights, car headlights, or electronic devices can suppress melatonin levels, making it harder to maintain deep, restorative sleep.

Blackout curtains are designed to block external light sources, creating a dark sleep environment that supports melatonin release and helps regulate circadian rhythms. Research has linked sleeping in a dark environment to improved sleep efficiency, increased REM sleep, and better overall health. Disrupted sleep due to light exposure has been associated with an increased risk of obesity, metabolic disorders, and mood disturbances. Health organizations like the National Sleep Foundation recommend reducing nighttime light exposure to enhance sleep quality and long-term well-being.

items.plain: Sleep on a mattress and pillow that feel comfortable to you.

items.evidenceSummary:
A good mattress and pillow are essential for maintaining proper spinal alignment, reducing pressure points, and promoting deep, uninterrupted sleep. Research shows that an uncomfortable or unsupportive sleep surface can contribute to musculoskeletal pain, frequent awakenings, and reduced sleep quality. Poor sleep due to an inadequate mattress has been linked to an increased risk of chronic pain, stress, and even cardiovascular issues.

Mattresses and pillows play a crucial role in regulating body temperature and pressure distribution during sleep. Memory foam, latex, and hybrid mattresses are known to provide better weight distribution, reducing tossing and turning throughout the night. Similarly, the right pillow supports the head and neck, preventing stiffness and discomfort that could disrupt sleep. Studies suggest that sleep surfaces tailored to an individual’s needs can improve sleep efficiency, decrease sleep disturbances, and enhance overall restfulness.

White noise machines can improve sleep quality by masking disruptive sounds and creating a consistent auditory environment. Research shows that unpredictable noises, such as traffic, barking dogs, or household activity, can cause frequent awakenings and fragmented sleep. White noise works by producing a steady sound that reduces the contrast between background noises, making sudden disturbances less likely to wake you.

Studies have demonstrated that white noise can shorten the time it takes to fall asleep, increase sleep efficiency, and enhance overall sleep satisfaction. In hospital settings, where noise pollution is a common issue, white noise has been shown to help patients sleep more soundly despite surrounding disturbances. Additionally, consistent sound exposure during sleep can improve slow-wave sleep, which is crucial for memory consolidation, immune function, and overall well-being.

items.plain: Do the same calm things in the same order before bed, like reading or a warm shower.
items.paragraph: Create a 30-minute wind-down routine before bed with calming activities like reading, light stretching, or listening to soft music. Stick to the same routine nightly to reinforce your body's sleep signals.
items.category: Sleep Hygiene (General Behavioral and Environmental Factors)
items.evidenceSummary:
A structured bedtime routine helps signal to the body that it’s time to wind down, making it easier to fall asleep and stay asleep. The brain relies on consistent cues to regulate melatonin production, the hormone responsible for sleep onset. Engaging in calming activities before bed promotes relaxation by reducing stress hormone levels, slowing the heart rate, and preparing the body for rest.

Research shows that engaging in a pre-sleep relaxation routine can improve sleep onset latency (the time it takes to fall asleep), sleep quality, and overall restfulness. Activities such as reading, taking a warm bath, or practicing deep breathing stimulate the parasympathetic nervous system, which counteracts stress and promotes relaxation. Additionally, avoiding stimulating activities—such as intense exercise, screen exposure, or work-related tasks—helps prevent disruptions to the body’s natural circadian rhythm.

NHLBI: 'Use the hour before bed for quiet time' and 'Take a hot bath or use relaxation techniques before bed.' SHF: 'Relax for an hour before going to bed.' AASM patient site: 'Establish a relaxing bedtime routine.'

Components include nutrition (feeding, healthy snack), hygiene (bathing, oral care), communication (reading, singing) and physical contact (massage, cuddling).

items.plain: Save exciting or stressful activities for earlier in the evening.
items.paragraph: Avoid intense exercise, heavy discussions, or engaging TV shows at least 1 hour before bed. Instead, opt for calming activities like gentle stretching, journaling, or deep breathing exercises.
items.category: Sleep Hygiene (General Behavioral and Environmental Factors)
items.evidenceSummary:
Engaging in stimulating activities before bedtime can interfere with the body's natural ability to wind down, making it harder to fall asleep. Activities that elevate heart rate, increase cognitive arousal, or trigger emotional responses can delay melatonin production and keep the brain in an alert state. Research indicates that exposure to psychological stress, intense exercise, or highly engaging content before sleep can increase cortisol levels and sympathetic nervous system activity, which counteract the relaxation needed for sleep onset.

Additionally, watching action-packed TV shows, engaging in heated discussions, or working late into the night can keep the brain highly active, delaying the transition into sleep. Studies have shown that excessive mental stimulation close to bedtime can lead to longer sleep onset latency, reduced sleep efficiency, and lighter sleep stages. This can negatively impact deep sleep and REM sleep, which are essential for cognitive function, memory consolidation, and emotional regulation.

items.plain: If you wake at night, don't look at the clock.
items.paragraph: Turn your clock away from your bed or use a non-illuminated alarm clock. If you wake up, focus on relaxing breathing exercises rather than checking the time.
items.category: Sleep Hygiene (General Behavioral and Environmental Factors)
items.evidenceSummary:
Clock-watching during nighttime awakenings can increase stress and make it harder to fall back asleep. When individuals check the time, they often begin calculating how much sleep they have left, which can lead to anxiety about insufficient rest. This heightened stress response activates the sympathetic nervous system, increasing cortisol levels and making relaxation more difficult.

Research has shown that sleep-related anxiety can significantly impact sleep quality. The more people focus on the time and worry about their sleep duration, the more likely they are to experience prolonged wakefulness. Additionally, exposure to bright or blue light from illuminated clocks or phone screens further suppresses melatonin production, delaying the return to sleep.

items.evidenceSummary:
Taking a warm shower or bath before bed can help regulate body temperature and promote sleep readiness. The process of warming the body and then cooling down mimics the natural drop in core temperature that occurs before sleep. This cooling effect signals the brain to produce melatonin, the hormone responsible for sleep onset.

Studies have shown that a warm bath or shower approximately 60–90 minutes before bedtime can improve sleep efficiency, decrease sleep onset latency (the time it takes to fall asleep), and enhance overall sleep quality. The heat from the water promotes vasodilation (expansion of blood vessels), which helps dissipate body heat and accelerate the body’s transition to a restful state.

items.evidenceSummary:
Pink noise, a type of sound with balanced lower frequencies, has been shown to enhance deep sleep by promoting slow-wave activity in the brain. Unlike white noise, which contains all frequencies at equal intensity, pink noise mimics natural ambient sounds such as rustling leaves, steady rain, or ocean waves, making it more soothing and less harsh on the ears.

Research suggests that exposure to pink noise during sleep can improve sleep stability, memory consolidation, and overall sleep quality. Studies have found that pink noise helps synchronize brain waves, allowing individuals to reach and maintain deeper sleep stages, which are essential for cognitive function and physical restoration. Compared to white noise, pink noise has been linked to a more restful and undisturbed sleep experience.

items.evidenceSummary:
Wearing socks to bed can improve sleep quality by promoting vasodilation, the widening of blood vessels, which helps regulate body temperature and signal to the body that it’s time to sleep. When the feet are warm, blood circulation improves, and heat is redistributed from the core to the extremities, facilitating the natural drop in core body temperature that occurs before sleep. This cooling effect helps the body transition into a sleep-ready state more efficiently.

Studies have shown that individuals who wear socks to bed fall asleep faster, stay asleep longer, and wake up less frequently during the night. Keeping the feet warm can also prevent discomfort caused by cold extremities, reducing sleep disturbances and improving overall sleep efficiency.

findings.keyResult: With feet-warming bed socks, sleep onset latency was on average 7.5 min shorter, total sleep time 32 min longer, number of awakenings 7.5 times smaller and sleep efficiency 7.6% higher (all P < 0.05); foot temperature was 1.3 °C higher. No difference in subjective sleep ratings.

citation.title: Effects of feet warming using bed socks on sleep quality and thermoregulatory responses in a cool environment.

items.plain: Use dimmer, warmer lights in the evening.
items.paragraph: Use blue light filter apps on screens, wear blue light-blocking glasses, and switch to warm, dim lighting (like red or amber bulbs) 1–2 hours before bed.
items.category: Physiological and Biological Factors Affecting Sleep

items.evidenceSummary:
Exposure to blue light from electronic devices (phones, tablets, computers, and TVs) in the evening can disrupt the body's natural sleep cycle by suppressing melatonin production, the hormone responsible for regulating sleep. Blue light has a short wavelength that stimulates the brain, keeping it alert and delaying sleep onset.

Research has shown that individuals exposed to blue light before bedtime experience delayed sleep onset, reduced sleep quality, and decreased REM sleep, which is crucial for cognitive function and emotional well-being. Minimizing blue light exposure at least 1–2 hours before bed can help regulate the body's circadian rhythm, promoting faster sleep onset and deeper rest.

sources.citation: Hartstein LE, Mathew GM, Reichenberger DA, et al. The impact of screen use on sleep health across the lifespan: A National Sleep Foundation consensus statement. Sleep Health. 2024;10(4):373-384.

findings.keyResult: Compared with dim light (<3 lux), room light (<200 lux) in the 8 h before bedtime suppressed melatonin, giving a later melatonin onset in 99.0% of individuals and shortening melatonin duration by about 90 min. Room light during usual sleep hours suppressed melatonin by greater than 50% in most (85%) trials.

citation.title: Exposure to room light before bedtime suppresses melatonin onset and shortens melatonin duration in humans.

findings.keyResult: Group-level ED50 for melatonin suppression was 24.60 lux. 10, 30 and 50 lux gave later apparent melatonin onsets by 22, 77 and 109 min. Individual ED50 ranged from 6 lux to 350 lux (26% coefficient of variation).

items.evidenceSummary:
Red light has the least impact on melatonin production and the body’s circadian rhythm compared to blue or white light. Unlike blue light, which suppresses melatonin and delays sleep onset, red light has longer wavelengths that do not interfere with the body's natural sleep cycle. Studies have shown that exposure to dim red light in the evening can help maintain optimal melatonin levels, promoting faster sleep onset, better sleep quality, and fewer nighttime awakenings.

Research also suggests that red light exposure before bed can enhance REM sleep and improve overall sleep efficiency, making it a beneficial alternative to bright artificial lighting at night.

items.plain: Try a few minutes of gentle stretching or yoga before bed.

items.category: Physiological and Biological Factors Affecting Sleep
items.evidenceSummary:
Engaging in gentle yoga or stretching before bed can help activate the parasympathetic nervous system, which promotes relaxation and prepares the body for sleep. Research shows that low-intensity movement, such as stretching or yoga, reduces cortisol (the stress hormone), eases muscle tension, and enhances melatonin production, all of which contribute to better sleep quality.

Yoga, in particular, has been found to increase slow-wave sleep (deep sleep) and REM sleep, both essential for physical restoration and cognitive function. Regular nighttime stretching or yoga can also improve sleep latency (time taken to fall asleep), reduce nighttime awakenings, and enhance overall sleep efficiency.

items.evidenceSummary:
Engaging in resistance training earlier in the day, particularly in the afternoon, has been linked to improved deep sleep quality and overall sleep efficiency. Studies suggest that strength training reduces sleep latency (the time it takes to fall asleep), increases time spent in slow-wave sleep (deep sleep), and enhances sleep duration.

Afternoon resistance training aligns with the body's natural fluctuations in hormone levels, such as cortisol and testosterone, optimizing performance and recovery. Compared to late-night workouts, which can elevate heart rate and core body temperature—potentially delaying sleep—afternoon sessions allow enough time for the body to cool down and transition smoothly into a sleep-ready state.

The 4-7-8 breathing technique is a controlled breathing exercise that helps activate the parasympathetic nervous system (PNS), which promotes relaxation and prepares the body for sleep. Research suggests that slow, deep breathing can lower heart rate, reduce blood pressure, and decrease cortisol levels, making it easier to transition into restful sleep.

This technique enhances vagal tone, which is associated with improved emotional regulation and stress resilience. By focusing on controlled breathing, individuals can shift attention away from racing thoughts, calm the nervous system, and reduce sleep latency (the time it takes to fall asleep).

items.evidenceSummary:
Breathing through the nose rather than the mouth during sleep is essential for optimal oxygen exchange, sleep quality, and overall health. Nasal breathing helps filter, warm, and humidify the air, reducing the risk of airway irritation and promoting efficient oxygen absorption. In contrast, chronic mouth breathing has been linked to lower oxygen saturation, increased snoring, disrupted sleep cycles, and even sleep apnea.

Research indicates that mouth breathing can contribute to dry mouth, increased risk of cavities, throat irritation, and a higher likelihood of waking up throughout the night. Additionally, nasal breathing supports the production of nitric oxide, a molecule that enhances oxygen delivery to cells, reduces inflammation, and improves cardiovascular function— all of which contribute to better sleep and overall well-being.

items.category: Physiological and Biological Factors Affecting Sleep
items.evidenceSummary:
Kiwi and tart cherries are natural sources of sleep-enhancing compounds, making them excellent bedtime snacks. Research suggests that both fruits can improve sleep duration and quality due to their high content of serotonin, melatonin, and antioxidants.

Kiwi is rich in serotonin, a neurotransmitter that regulates sleep-wake cycles and promotes relaxation. It also contains high levels of vitamin C and antioxidants, which help reduce inflammation and oxidative stress, both of which can negatively impact sleep. Studies have shown that consuming kiwi one hour before bed can shorten sleep onset, reduce nighttime awakenings, and increase total sleep time.

Tart cherries are a natural source of melatonin, the hormone responsible for regulating circadian rhythms. Consuming tart cherry juice or whole cherries before bed has been linked to increased melatonin levels, improved sleep efficiency, and longer sleep duration. Their anti-inflammatory properties may also help reduce discomfort that can disrupt sleep.

findings.keyResult: After 4 weeks of 2 kiwifruit 1 hour before bedtime, PSQI score, wake after sleep onset and sleep onset latency decreased by 42.4%, 28.9% and 35.4%; total sleep time and sleep efficiency increased by 13.4% and 5.41%.

items.evidenceSummary:
Consuming a light carbohydrate-rich snack before bed can help promote serotonin production and improve sleep quality. Carbohydrates facilitate the uptake of tryptophan, an amino acid that serves as a precursor to serotonin and melatonin, both of which regulate sleep. Studies suggest that low-glycemic, carb-containing snacks can shorten sleep onset and enhance sleep efficiency by promoting relaxation and stabilizing blood sugar levels overnight.

- Bananas are a great bedtime snack because they contain magnesium, potassium, and vitamin B6, which aid in muscle relaxation and serotonin production. - Almond butter provides healthy fats and a small amount of protein, helping to balance blood sugar levels and prevent nighttime awakenings caused by hunger. - Oatmeal, whole grain toast, or a handful of nuts are also effective options for sustaining energy levels without causing digestive discomfort.

items.evidenceSummary:
Chamomile and passionflower tea are well-known for their mild sedative effects, which help promote relaxation and improve sleep quality. Chamomile contains apigenin, a flavonoid that binds to GABA receptors in the brain, producing calming and anti-anxiety effects. Studies have shown that chamomile tea can help reduce nighttime awakenings, improve sleep efficiency, and promote relaxation. Passionflower also enhances GABA activity, reducing brain excitability and helping the body transition into a restful state. Research suggests that drinking passionflower tea before bed can improve overall sleep quality and reduce insomnia symptoms.

Both teas are caffeine-free and have been traditionally used as natural sleep aids, making them excellent alternatives to pharmaceutical sleep medications.

findings.keyResult: Chamomile significantly reduced PSQI score (WMD: -1.88, 95% CI: -3.46, -0.31, I2: 88.4%, n = 5). Sleep onset latency improved in three of four studies and night awakenings in two of three; sleep efficiency and daytime functioning did not improve. No adverse events reported.

While stress management is well-supported as a sleep aid, the best methods remain debated, and some interventions require more research.

items.evidenceSummary:
Engaging in relaxation techniques before bed can help activate the parasympathetic nervous system, reducing stress and preparing the body for sleep.

- Deep breathing exercises (such as diaphragmatic breathing or the 4-7-8 technique) have been shown to slow heart rate, lower blood pressure, and reduce cortisol levels, promoting a state of calm that makes it easier to fall asleep. - Meditation and mindfulness practices can help quiet a racing mind, reduce nighttime anxiety, and improve sleep latency (the time it takes to fall asleep). Studies suggest that mindfulness meditation can enhance sleep efficiency and reduce symptoms of insomnia by promoting relaxation and increasing melatonin levels. - Progressive muscle relaxation (PMR), where different muscle groups are tensed and then released, can reduce physical tension and promote deeper sleep.

By calming the nervous system and reducing mental stimulation, relaxation techniques help counteract stress-induced insomnia and improve overall sleep quality.

Progressive Muscle Relaxation (PMR) is a proven technique that helps reduce physical tension, lower stress levels, and improve sleep onset.

- PMR works by systematically tensing and then relaxing different muscle groups, helping the body recognize and release stored tension. - Research shows that PMR can lower heart rate, decrease blood pressure, and reduce cortisol levels, all of which contribute to better sleep. - Studies have found that individuals who practice PMR regularly experience faster sleep onset, fewer nighttime awakenings, and improved overall sleep quality.

By promoting deep relaxation and calming the nervous system, PMR helps the body transition into a restful state, making it easier to fall and stay asleep.

items.evidenceSummary:
Using the bed exclusively for sleep and intimacy reinforces a strong mental association between the bedroom environment and restful sleep.

- According to sleep hygiene principles, engaging in other activities like watching TV, working, or scrolling on a phone in bed can weaken the brain’s connection between the bed and sleep, making it harder to fall and stay asleep. - Studies show that conditioning the brain to associate the bed only with sleep helps regulate the body’s circadian rhythm, making it easier to fall asleep naturally. - Sleep researchers emphasize that avoiding stimulating activities in bed reduces sleep-onset latency (time it takes to fall asleep) and improves overall sleep efficiency.

By reserving the bed for sleep and intimacy, you reinforce a healthy sleep environment and minimize distractions that can interfere with restful sleep.

Engaging in cognitive shuffling mimics the mind’s natural transition into sleep, shifting the brain from structured thought patterns to a more dream-like, fragmented state that encourages drowsiness. Studies on sleep and cognitive distraction techniques show that disrupting logical thought processes reduces sleep-onset latency and promotes faster sleep induction.

Research suggests that listening to low-frequency binaural beats (2-8 Hz, in the delta and theta ranges) may help promote deep relaxation, reduce stress, and improve sleep quality. Delta waves (0.5-4 Hz) are associated with deep sleep, while theta waves (4-8 Hz) are linked to drowsiness and early sleep stages. Some studies indicate that binaural beats may enhance slow-wave sleep, the most restorative stage of sleep, by encouraging brainwave synchronization with these frequencies.

items.paragraph: If you experience acid reflux at night, try placing a wedge pillow under your upper body while sleeping on your left side for added relief.
items.category: Medical and Pharmacological Considerations
items.evidenceSummary: Sleeping on your left side has been shown to promote better digestion and reduce acid reflux, particularly for individuals with gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) or frequent heartburn. Studies indicate that left-side sleeping helps keep the stomach positioned below the esophagus, preventing acid from traveling back up into the throat. This is due to the natural orientation of the stomach and esophageal sphincter, which makes reflux less likely in this position. In contrast, sleeping on the right side can relax the lower esophageal sphincter, potentially worsening acid reflux symptoms.

findings.keyResult: Left-side sleeping reduced acid exposure time vs right side (MD -2.03) and vs supine (MD -2.71) and shortened acid clearance time; one RCT of a positional device improved night-time symptoms and reflux-free nights.

citation.title: Left lateral decubitus sleeping position is associated with improved gastroesophageal reflux disease symptoms: A systematic review and meta-analysis.

findings.population: 100 patients with nocturnal GERD symptoms; double-blind sham-controlled
findings.keyResult: Treatment success (≥50% fall in nocturnal reflux score) was 44% with the device vs 24% with sham (risk difference 20%; 95% CI 1.8%-38.2%; P = .03). Time on the left side rose to 60.9% vs 38.5%; reflux-free nights 9 vs 6.

citation.title: Sleep Positional Therapy for Nocturnal Gastroesophageal Reflux: A Double-Blind, Randomized, Sham-Controlled Trial.

items.plain: Some people relax with gentle massage or acupressure before sleep.
items.paragraph: Try gently massaging the pericardium-6 point (three finger-widths below your wrist crease) in circular motions for one to two minutes before bed to promote relaxation.
items.category: Medical and Pharmacological Considerations
items.audienceNote: Acupressure points (P6) come from traditional Chinese medicine.
items.evidenceSummary: Acupressure and gentle massage have been shown to promote relaxation, reduce stress, and improve sleep quality. Research suggests that stimulating specific pressure points—such as the Pericardium-6 (P6) point on the inner wrist or the Yintang point between the eyebrows—can help calm the nervous system, lower heart rate, and encourage melatonin production. Acupressure works by stimulating energy pathways (meridians) in the body, much like acupuncture, but without the use of needles. Studies indicate that regular acupressure can reduce insomnia symptoms, shorten sleep onset time, and enhance sleep depth.

items.plain: If you have reflux or sleep apnea, raising your upper body may help; ask your clinician.
items.paragraph: For best results, elevate your upper body by 6-8 inches using a wedge pillow or an adjustable bed instead of stacking pillows, which can strain the neck.
items.category: Medical and Pharmacological Considerations
items.evidenceSummary: Sleeping in a slightly inclined position has been shown to improve breathing, reduce acid reflux, and enhance overall sleep quality. Studies indicate that elevating the upper body by about 6–8 inches can help prevent airway collapse in people with obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), reducing snoring and breathing disruptions. For those with gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) or occasional heartburn, an elevated position prevents stomach acid from flowing back into the esophagus, lowering discomfort and improving sleep continuity.

findings.keyResult: 'We suggest elevating head of bed for nighttime GERD symptoms' (conditional recommendation, low level of evidence). The text notes several RCTs showed improvement in nocturnal symptoms and acid exposure with head-of-bed elevation or a wedge, and that lying right-side down increases nocturnal reflux compared with left-side down.

citation.title: ACG Clinical Guideline for the Diagnosis and Management of Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease.

findings.keyResult: Lifestyle studies included head-of-bed elevation (n = 5), longer dinner-to-bed time (n = 2) and left-side positioning (n = 2). Authors recommend a stepwise strategy: head-of-bed elevation, longer dinner-to-bed interval, left-side sleeping, then acid-suppressive medicine.

citation.title: Systematic review: Clinical effectiveness of interventions for the treatment of nocturnal gastroesophageal reflux.

findings.population: 52 OSA patients, single clinic, before-after polysomnography
findings.keyResult: Head-of-bed elevation of 7.5° lowered AHI from 15.7 [11.3-22.5] to 10.7 [6.6-16.5] events/h (p < 0.001) and raised minimum oxygen saturation from 83.5 to 87% (p = 0.003), without changing sleep architecture.

citation.title: The influence of head-of-bed elevation in patients with obstructive sleep apnea.

items.plain: Some people find raising their legs a little helps them feel comfortable at night.
items.category: Medical and Pharmacological Considerations

items.plain: Write down when you go to bed, wake up and how you slept for a week or two.
items.paragraph: Use a notebook or sleep-tracking app to record your bedtime, wake time, sleep interruptions, and factors like caffeine intake or stress levels for at least two weeks to spot trends.
items.category: Medical and Pharmacological Considerations
items.evidenceSummary: Keeping a sleep diary is a widely recommended tool for identifying sleep disturbances and improving sleep quality. Sleep specialists, including those at the National Sleep Foundation and American Academy of Sleep Medicine, often use sleep diaries to track sleep patterns, detect underlying sleep disorders, and evaluate the effectiveness of sleep interventions. Studies show that individuals who maintain a sleep log gain better insight into their sleep habits, which helps them identify and correct behaviors that may be negatively affecting their rest. A sleep diary can be especially helpful for diagnosing conditions like insomnia, delayed sleep phase disorder, or sleep apnea.

findings.population: adults; good sleepers, insomnia, sleep apnea (focus groups)
findings.keyResult: Expert consensus and patient focus groups produced the Consensus Sleep Diary (Core and expanded versions); Core diary written at a third-grade reading level and instructions at a sixth-grade level.

citation.authors: Carney CE, Buysse DJ, Ancoli-Israel S, et al.
citation.title: The consensus sleep diary: standardizing prospective sleep self-monitoring.

findings.keyResult: Recommended diagnostic procedure: clinical interview, sleep questionnaires and diaries (grade A). Actigraphy not recommended for routine evaluation (C).

citation.authors: Riemann D, Espie CA, Altena E, et al.
citation.title: The European Insomnia Guideline: An update on the diagnosis and treatment of insomnia 2023.

items.plain: If you can't fall asleep until very late, ask a clinician about timed melatonin or morning light.
items.plainBefore: If you can't fall asleep until very late, ask a clinician about morning bright-light therapy.
items.paragraph: If you struggle with falling asleep late and waking up late, use a 10,000-lux light box for 30 minutes within an hour of waking up to help regulate your circadian rhythm.
items.category: Medical and Pharmacological Considerations
items.evidenceSummary: Light therapy is a clinically proven treatment for Delayed Sleep Phase Disorder (DSPD), a condition where an individual's internal clock is shifted later than the typical sleep schedule. Research shows that exposure to bright light in the morning helps regulate the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN)—the brain’s master clock—by suppressing melatonin production earlier in the day, making it easier to fall asleep at an appropriate time. The American Academy of Sleep Medicine and other sleep experts recommend light therapy as a non-pharmacological approach to correcting circadian rhythm misalignment.

findings.keyResult: AASM 2015: 'There is insufficient evidence to support efficacy of post-awakening light therapy (monotherapy) as a treatment for DSWPD (versus no treatment). No recommendation.' For children and adolescents: post-awakening light therapy in conjunction with behavioral treatments [WEAK FOR]. For adults with and without depression: strategically timed melatonin [WEAK FOR].

citation.title: Clinical Practice Guideline for the Treatment of Intrinsic Circadian Rhythm Sleep-Wake Disorders: ASWPD, DSWPD, N24SWD, and ISWRD. An Update for 2015: An American Academy of Sleep Medicine Clinical Practice Guideline.

findings.keyResult: Light therapy was effective for sleep problems in general (g = 0.39), circadian rhythm sleep disorders (g = 0.41), insomnia (g = 0.47) and dementia-related sleep problems (g = 0.30). For circadian rhythm sleep disorders, effects were smaller in RCTs. Indication of publication bias; most effects small to medium.

citation.title: The effects of light therapy on sleep problems: A systematic review and meta-analysis.

findings.population: people with intrinsic circadian rhythm sleep-wake disorders
findings.keyResult: AASM 2015 (GRADE): positive endorsement (second-tier confidence) of strategically timed melatonin for DSWPD, blind adults with N24SWD, and children/adolescents with ISWRD and neurological disorders; and light therapy with or without behavioral interventions for adults with ASWPD, children/adolescents with DSWPD, and elderly with dementia. Recommendations against melatonin and sleep-promoting medications for demented elderly patients.

citation.title: Clinical Practice Guideline for the Treatment of Intrinsic Circadian Rhythm Sleep-Wake Disorders: ASWPD, DSWPD, N24SWD, and ISWRD. An Update for 2015

findings.population: older adults with primary insomnia (n = 51, aged 63.6 ± 7.1)
findings.keyResult: 12-week program of sleep hygiene plus 45 min daily bright (~4,000 lux) or dim (~65 lux) light, morning or evening. Subjective and objective sleep changes after bright light were not significantly different from dim light, though light shifted circadian phase predictably.

citation.authors: Friedman L, Zeitzer JM, Kushida C, et al.
citation.title: Scheduled bright light for treatment of insomnia in older adults.

items.plain: Melatonin may help with jet lag or shift work; ask a pharmacist or doctor first.
items.category: Medical and Pharmacological Considerations
items.audienceNote: Melatonin is sold over the counter in some countries and by prescription in others.

positions.says: Discusses melatonin for jet lag but says the evidence is mixed (pp. 10-12).

findings.population: adults with DSWPD and delayed melatonin rhythm (n = 116, mean age 29.0)
findings.keyResult: 0.5 mg fast-release melatonin 1 h before desired bedtime plus behavioural sleep scheduling for 4 weeks: sleep onset 34 min earlier (95% CI -60 to -8) vs placebo; more patients had more than minimal clinician-rated improvement (52.8% vs 24.0%). Adverse events similar between groups.

citation.title: Efficacy of melatonin with behavioural sleep-wake scheduling for delayed sleep-wake phase disorder: A double-blind, randomised clinical trial.

findings.keyResult: Maximum phase advances occurred when 0.5 mg melatonin was taken in the afternoon, 2-4 h before dim light melatonin onset, or 9-11 h before sleep midpoint. The optimal time is later for 0.5 mg than for 3.0 mg; at their optimal times both doses yield similarly sized advances and delays.

citation.title: Human phase response curves to three days of daily melatonin: 0.5 mg versus 3.0 mg.

findings.keyResult: Nine of ten trials found melatonin taken close to target bedtime at the destination (10pm to midnight) decreased jet lag from flights crossing five or more time zones. Doses of 0.5 to 5mg similarly effective; 5mg gave faster sleep onset; above 5mg no more effective. NNT is 2. If taken at the wrong time (early in the day) it can cause sleepiness and delay adaptation. Case reports suggest people with epilepsy and patients taking warfarin may come to harm.

citation.title: Melatonin for the prevention and treatment of jet lag.

findings.keyResult: Melatonin (1 to 10 mg) after the night shift may increase daytime sleep length (MD 24 minutes, 95% CI 9.8 to 38.9; 7 trials, 263 participants, low quality) and night-time sleep (MD 17 minutes, 95% CI 3.71 to 30.22) but not sleep latency. Caffeine plus pre-shift naps decreased sleepiness (KSS MD -0.63, 95% CI -1.09 to -0.17; one trial). Armodafinil/modafinil reduce sleepiness in shift work sleep disorder but have adverse events.

citation.title: Pharmacological interventions for sleepiness and sleep disturbances caused by shift work.

findings.keyResult: AASM 2017 pharmacologic guideline: 'We suggest that clinicians not use melatonin as a treatment for sleep onset or sleep maintenance insomnia (versus no treatment) in adults. (WEAK).' Same weak 'not use' suggestion for trazodone, tiagabine, diphenhydramine, tryptophan and valerian.

items.plain: If you snore loudly or gasp in your sleep, ask a doctor about sleep apnea.
items.category: Medical and Pharmacological Considerations

findings.population: adults with signs and symptoms of OSA
findings.keyResult: AASM: polysomnography is the standard test when a comprehensive sleep evaluation raises concern for OSA. Questionnaires and prediction tools should not be used to diagnose OSA without polysomnography or home sleep apnea testing (STRONG). Polysomnography or a technically adequate home test is recommended for uncomplicated adults with signs and symptoms of moderate-to-severe OSA (STRONG).

citation.title: Clinical Practice Guideline for Diagnostic Testing for Adult Obstructive Sleep Apnea: An American Academy of Sleep Medicine Clinical Practice Guideline.

findings.population: asymptomatic adults and adults with unrecognized symptoms
findings.keyResult: USPSTF: current evidence is insufficient to assess the balance of benefits and harms of screening for OSA in the general adult population (I statement). Estimated prevalence of moderate-to-severe OSA (AHI ≥15) was 13% in men and 6% in women.

citation.authors: US Preventive Services Task Force (Mangione CM, et al.)
citation.title: Screening for Obstructive Sleep Apnea in Adults: US Preventive Services Task Force Recommendation Statement.

items.plain: Ask your pharmacist or doctor whether any of your medicines can affect sleep.
items.paragraph: Some heart, blood pressure, and asthma medicines, along with some over-the-counter cough, cold, and allergy remedies, can interfere with sleep. If you're having trouble sleeping, ask your doctor or pharmacist whether something you're taking could be the cause, and whether it can be taken earlier in the day instead.
items.category: Medical and Pharmacological Considerations

items.plain: For long-lasting insomnia, ask about CBT-I, a structured talking and habits treatment.
items.paragraph: A structured treatment for chronic insomnia that combines behavior changes — like reconditioning and sleep restriction therapy — with replacing unhelpful thoughts about sleep, such as "I'll never fall asleep without pills," with more realistic ones. It's effective for most people with chronic insomnia.
items.category: Medical and Pharmacological Considerations

findings.keyResult: AASM 2021 (GRADE): 'We recommend that clinicians use multicomponent cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia for the treatment of chronic insomnia disorder in adults. (STRONG).' Also conditional recommendations for multicomponent brief therapies, stimulus control, sleep restriction therapy and relaxation therapy. 66 RCTs comparing CBT-I to wait-list, minimal or placebo therapies were identified.

citation.authors: Edinger JD, Arnedt JT, Bertisch SM, et al.
citation.title: Behavioral and psychological treatments for chronic insomnia disorder in adults: an American Academy of Sleep Medicine clinical practice guideline

findings.keyResult: ACP recommends that all adult patients receive CBT-I as the initial treatment for chronic insomnia disorder (strong recommendation, moderate-quality evidence). Medication only via shared decision-making if CBT-I alone was unsuccessful (weak recommendation, low-quality evidence).

citation.title: Management of Chronic Insomnia Disorder in Adults: A Clinical Practice Guideline From the American College of Physicians

findings.keyResult: ESRS 2017: CBT-I is recommended as the first-line treatment for chronic insomnia in adults of any age (strong recommendation, high-quality evidence). Pharmacological intervention can be offered if CBT-I is not sufficiently effective or not available; benzodiazepines, BZRAs and some antidepressants effective short-term (≤4 weeks; weak recommendation). Antihistamines, antipsychotics, melatonin and phytotherapeutics are not recommended. Light therapy and exercise need further evaluation (weak, low-quality evidence). Homeopathy and acupuncture not recommended.

citation.title: European guideline for the diagnosis and treatment of insomnia

findings.population: adults with chronic insomnia, including with comorbidities
findings.keyResult: ESRS 2023: CBT-I is recommended as first-line treatment for chronic insomnia in adults of any age (including patients with comorbidities), either in-person or digitally (A). Prolonged-release melatonin can be used for up to 3 months in patients ≥ 55 years (B); fast-release melatonin, antihistamines, antipsychotics, ramelteon and phytotherapeutics are not recommended (A). Light therapy and exercise may be useful as adjunct therapies to CBT-I (B). Actigraphy not recommended for routine evaluation (C).

citation.title: The European Insomnia Guideline: An update on the diagnosis and treatment of insomnia 2023

findings.keyResult: Strong recommendation for multicomponent CBT-I; conditional recommendations for multicomponent brief therapies, stimulus control alone, sleep restriction alone and relaxation therapy alone; conditional recommendation against sleep hygiene as a single-component therapy. Based on GRADE review of 124 included studies (89 analysed) in the companion review (PMID 33164741).

citation.authors: Edinger JD, Arnedt JT, Bertisch SM, et al.
citation.title: Behavioral and psychological treatments for chronic insomnia disorder in adults: an American Academy of Sleep Medicine clinical practice guideline.

findings.keyResult: ACP recommends that all adult patients receive CBT-I as the initial treatment for chronic insomnia disorder (strong recommendation, moderate-quality evidence); medication added via shared decision-making only if CBT-I alone was unsuccessful (weak recommendation, low-quality evidence).

citation.authors: Qaseem A, Kansagara D, Forciea MA, et al.
citation.title: Management of Chronic Insomnia Disorder in Adults: A Clinical Practice Guideline From the American College of Physicians.

findings.population: adults of any age with chronic insomnia, including with comorbidities
findings.keyResult: CBT-I recommended as first-line treatment for chronic insomnia in adults of any age (including patients with comorbidities), either in-person or digitally (grade A). Pharmacological treatment can be offered when CBT-I is not sufficiently effective (A).

citation.authors: Riemann D, Espie CA, Altena E, et al.
citation.title: The European Insomnia Guideline: An update on the diagnosis and treatment of insomnia 2023.

findings.population: adults with chronic insomnia without comorbidity
findings.keyResult: 20 RCTs (1162 participants). Post-treatment: sleep onset latency improved by 19.03 (95% CI 14.12 to 23.93) minutes, WASO by 26.00 (15.48 to 36.52) minutes, total sleep time by 7.61 (-0.51 to 15.74) minutes, sleep efficiency by 9.91% (8.09% to 11.73%). No adverse outcomes reported.

citation.authors: Trauer JM, Qian MY, Doyle JS, et al.
citation.title: Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Chronic Insomnia: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis.

findings.keyResult: 33 RCTs; 4719 dCBT-I vs 4645 control. ISI mean difference -5.00 (95% CI -5.68 to -4.33) post-intervention; -3.99 (-4.82 to -3.16) short-term follow-up; -3.48 (-4.21 to -2.76) at 1 year. Face-to-face CBT-I produced greater improvement than dCBT-I (3.07, 95% CI 1.18 to 4.95), within a 4-point non-inferiority margin.

citation.authors: Soh HL, Ho RC, Ho CS, et al.
citation.title: Efficacy of digital cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia: a meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials.

findings.population: adults with self-reported insomnia symptoms (online sample, 91.1% white, 77.7% female)
findings.keyResult: 1711 participants; dCBT vs sleep hygiene education. Small improvement in functional health (week 24 adjusted difference 1.76, 95% CI 1.22-2.30) and psychological well-being (2.95, 2.13-3.76), large improvement in sleep-related quality of life (-18.72, -22.04 to -15.41). Insomnia improvement mediated 45.5%-84.0% of effects.

citation.authors: Espie CA, Emsley R, Kyle SD, et al.
citation.title: Effect of Digital Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Insomnia on Health, Psychological Well-being, and Sleep-Related Quality of Life: A Randomized Clinical Trial.

findings.keyResult: Remission vs control: individual OR = 8.36 (k = 36), group OR = 4.65 (k = 22), fully automated internet OR = 3.87 (k = 50), supported internet OR = 8.35 (k = 19). Completion of all sessions: individual 83.8%, supported internet 70.7%, fully automated internet 58.4%.

citation.title: Remission, treatment response, and treatment adherence across the delivery methods of cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.

findings.keyResult: 20 RCTs. Self-help CBT improved sleep, sleep-related cognitions, anxiety and depression. Effect sizes at post-treatment: sleep efficiency 0.80, sleep onset latency 0.66, WASO 0.55. Dropout 14.5% vs 16.7% for therapist-administered CBT. Telephone consultation added benefit.

citation.authors: Ho FY, Chung KF, Yeung WF, et al.
citation.title: Self-help cognitive-behavioral therapy for insomnia: a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.

findings.population: adults with poor sleep or insomnia
findings.keyResult: 15 studies; 12 compared sleep hygiene education (SHE) with CBT-I. SHE gave small-to-medium pre-post improvements but was significantly less efficacious than CBT-I (medium to large difference); SHE-CBT-I difference averaged 8% in diary sleep efficiency and two PSQI points.

citation.authors: Chung KF, Lee CT, Yeung WF, et al.
citation.title: Sleep hygiene education as a treatment of insomnia: a systematic review and meta-analysis.

findings.keyResult: AASM suggests CBT-I plus medication over medication alone (conditional, low certainty), and suggests against CBT-I plus medication over CBT-I alone (conditional, low certainty).

citation.authors: Buysse DJ, Arnedt JT, Buenaver L, et al.
citation.title: Combination treatment for chronic insomnia disorder in adults: an American Academy of Sleep Medicine clinical practice guideline.

findings.population: perimenopausal and postmenopausal women aged 40-65 with insomnia and hot flashes (n = 106)
findings.keyResult: At 8 weeks ISI scores decreased 9.9 points with telephone CBT-I vs 4.7 with menopause education, between-group difference 5.2 points; PSQI between-group difference 2.7 points. At 8 and 24 weeks, 70% and 84% of CBT-I participants were in the no-insomnia range vs 24% and 43% of controls. Hot flash frequency did not differ, but hot flash interference fell more with CBT-I.

citation.authors: McCurry SM, Guthrie KA, Morin CM, et al.
citation.title: Telephone-Based Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Insomnia in Perimenopausal and Postmenopausal Women With Vasomotor Symptoms: A MsFLASH Randomized Clinical Trial.

findings.population: adults with insomnia and a comorbid mental disorder (22 RCTs)
findings.keyResult: Effect sizes for insomnia severity reduction: 0.5 (CI 0.3-0.8) depression, 1.5 (CI 1.0-1.9) PTSD, 1.4 (CI 0.9-1.9) alcohol dependency, 1.2 (CI 0.8-1.7) psychosis/bipolar, 0.8 (CI 0.1-1.6) mixed. Comorbid symptom reduction post-treatment: 0.5 (CI 0.1-0.8) depression, 1.3 (CI 0.6-1.9) PTSD; no significant effects on comorbid symptoms at follow-up.

findings.population: college students and young adults aged 18-25 (13 RCTs, 5251 participants)
findings.keyResult: Digital interventions (CBT-I, mindfulness, sleep education via web or app) improved sleep quality (Hedges g=-1.25), sleep efficiency (g=0.62), insomnia severity (g=-4.08), dysfunctional beliefs (g=-1.54), sleep hygiene (g=-0.19) and sleep knowledge. Evidence certainty moderate to very low; very high heterogeneity (I2 up to 99%).

citation.authors: Lu YA, Lin HC, Tsai PS
citation.title: Effects of Digital Sleep Interventions on Sleep Among College Students and Young Adults: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.

findings.keyResult: Sleep hygiene education improved ISI from pre- to post-treatment (MD 3.4, 95% CI 2.08-4.64) but was inferior to CBT-I (MD 3.8), partial CBT-I (MD 4.5), exercise (MD 2.9) and acupressure (MD 1.9). 85.71% of trials had high risk of bias.

citation.authors: Ruan JY, Liu Q, Chung KF, et al.
citation.title: Effects of sleep hygiene education for insomnia: A systematic review and meta-analysis.

items.plain: With a clinician's help, limit time in bed to the sleep you actually get, then add time back.
items.paragraph: A technique for insomnia that limits time in bed to match how much you actually sleep. Calculate your average sleep time over a week, keep your time in bed to that amount, then gradually add more as your sleep improves. Naps longer than 15-20 minutes are avoided during this process, since they can undo the effect.

findings.keyResult: AASM 2021: 'We suggest that clinicians use sleep restriction therapy as a single-component therapy for the treatment of chronic insomnia disorder in adults. (CONDITIONAL).' Defined as limiting time in bed to the patient's sleep duration (from daily diaries), then increasing or decreasing based on sleep efficiency thresholds.

citation.authors: Edinger JD, Arnedt JT, Bertisch SM, et al.
citation.title: Behavioral and psychological treatments for chronic insomnia disorder in adults: an American Academy of Sleep Medicine clinical practice guideline

findings.keyResult: Sleep restriction iOR for remission 1.49 (95% CI 1.04-2.13); associated with improved subjective sleep quality, sleep efficiency and wake after sleep onset.

citation.authors: Furukawa Y, Sakata M, Yamamoto R, et al.
citation.title: Components and Delivery Formats of Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Chronic Insomnia in Adults: A Systematic Review and Component Network Meta-Analysis.

findings.population: adults with insomnia disorder, 35 English general practices
findings.keyResult: 642 participants. At 6 months ISI was 10.9 (SD 5.5) with sleep restriction vs 13.9 (5.2) with sleep hygiene booklet (adjusted mean difference -3.05, 95% CI -3.83 to -2.28; Cohen's d -0.74). Incremental cost per QALY £2076. Eight serious adverse events per group, none judged related to the intervention.

citation.authors: Kyle SD, Siriwardena AN, Espie CA, et al.
citation.title: Clinical and cost-effectiveness of nurse-delivered sleep restriction therapy for insomnia in primary care (HABIT): a pragmatic, superiority, open-label, randomised controlled trial.

findings.keyResult: AASM suggests that clinicians use sleep restriction therapy as a single-component therapy for chronic insomnia disorder in adults (CONDITIONAL).
