citation.title: Behavioral and psychological treatments for chronic insomnia disorder in adults: an American Academy of Sleep Medicine clinical practice guideline.

items.plain: Before a long trip, shift your sleep times a little toward the new time zone.
items.paragraph: A handful of adjustments that can ease jet lag on a trip of more than a few days: shift your sleep and wake times by small steps for a couple of days beforehand, get plenty of outdoor daylight right after you arrive, skip alcohol and afternoon caffeine, and keep any naps short (10-15 minutes).
items.category: Sleep Hygiene (General Behavioral and Environmental Factors)

findings.population: adults with circadian rhythm sleep disorders (AASM)
findings.keyResult: Planned sleep schedules are indicated in SWD (Standard) and JLD (Option); timed light exposure is indicated for each circadian disorder 'with variable success' (Option); timed melatonin is indicated for JLD (Standard) and SWD (Guideline); hypnotics may be indicated for daytime sleep among night shift workers (Guideline) and jet-lag insomnia (Option).

citation.title: Practice parameters for the clinical evaluation and treatment of circadian rhythm sleep disorders. An American Academy of Sleep Medicine report.

findings.keyResult: Advancing sleep 1 h/day for 3 days with morning bright light for 3.5 h after waking advanced DLMO by 2.1 h (continuous) or 1.5 h (intermittent), vs 0.6 h in dim light. Side effects were small.

citation.title: Preflight adjustment to eastward travel: 3 days of advancing sleep with and without morning bright light.

items.plain: On night shifts, use bright light at work and a dark, quiet room to sleep in.
items.paragraph: Ways to make night-shift sleep easier: add naps and extra sleep time, use bright light at work, keep shift changes infrequent so your body clock has time to adjust, block out light and noise while sleeping during the day, and limit caffeine to the start of the shift.
items.category: Sleep Hygiene (General Behavioral and Environmental Factors)

findings.population: shift workers who work nights (17 RCTs, 556 participants)
findings.keyResult: Bright light during the night reduced sleepiness on the Stanford Sleepiness Scale by 0.83 points (95% CI -1.3 to -0.36; 2 studies, 184 participants, very low quality). A single night-shift nap reduced reaction time by 11.87 ms (95% CI 31.94 to -8.2, very low quality). Authors: not possible to determine whether sleepiness or sleep can be improved with these interventions.

citation.title: Person-directed, non-pharmacological interventions for sleepiness at work and sleep disturbances caused by shift work.

findings.keyResult: Light therapy improved total sleep time (MD = 32.54, p < 0.00001) and sleep efficiency (MD = 2.91, p = 0.007) vs control. Medium illuminance (900-6000 lx) for >= 1 h during night was more effective for total sleep time.

citation.title: A systematic review and meta-analysis on light therapy for sleep disorders in shift workers.

findings.population: real or simulated night-shift workers (5 studies)
findings.keyResult: Evening light produced phase delays in melatonin, body temperature and sleep propensity and improved sleep quality, sleep duration, memory and work performance; no negative effects. Confidence moderate for circadian phase markers to very low for mood.

citation.title: The effect of evening light on circadian-related outcomes: A systematic review.

findings.population: working-age adults (18 studies, 494 participants; 6 real-work, 12 lab)
findings.keyResult: Mean nap 41.6 ± 28.3 min, at mean 2.12 am. Overall improvement after a nap vs no nap (effect size 0.25, 0.10 to 0.41). Earlier naps in the night tended to help more (-0.57, -1.16 to 0.002). Improvements mainly 30 min after awakening; memory worsened immediately after waking.

citation.title: Napping and cognitive performance during night shifts: a systematic review and meta-analysis.

findings.keyResult: NHLBI shift-work tips: take naps and raise the amount of time available for sleep; keep the lights bright at work; limit shift changes so your body clock can adjust; limit caffeine use to the first part of your shift; remove sound and light distractions in your bedroom during daytime sleep (for example, use light-blocking curtains).

citation.authors: National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NIH)
citation.title: Healthy Sleep Habits (last updated March 24, 2022)

findings.keyResult: 84% of experts agreed tailored guidelines were needed for shift workers. 18 consensus guidelines, including: aim for 7-9 hours per 24 hours, possibly split into a main sleep plus shorter sleeps; a sleep schedule per shift type; sleep somewhere cool (16-20ºC/60-68ºF), dark and quiet; wear sunglasses driving home after night shift; caffeine can help before and during a shift; avoid nicotine entirely or within 6 hours of bed; limit food on night shifts; regular exercise, noting that nighttime exercise doesn't disrupt sleep for most people.

citation.authors: Shriane AE, Rigney G, Ferguson SA, et al.
citation.title: Healthy sleep practices for shift workers: consensus sleep hygiene guidelines using a Delphi methodology.

findings.population: rotating night shift workers (30 studies; 25 in meta-analysis)
findings.keyResult: Interventions grouped as pharmacological (n = 7), light therapy (n = 9), cognitive behavioural (n = 7), aroma or alternative therapy (n = 4) and shift schedule modification (n = 3). Overall mean effect size moderate (Hedges' g = 0.59; 95% CI 0.33-0.84).

citation.authors: Jeon BM, Kim SH, Shin SH
citation.title: Effectiveness of sleep interventions for rotating night shift workers: a systematic review and meta-analysis.

items.plain: Some advise getting outside in late-afternoon light too.
items.paragraph: Spend a little time outdoors in the late afternoon or early evening, when the sun is low, looking toward the sky (never straight at the sun). It is meant to signal to your body clock that evening is coming.
items.category: Physiological and Biological Factors Affecting Sleep
items.subcategory: Light Exposure and Circadian Rhythm Regulation

findings.keyResult: No study found that tested late-afternoon light for sleep in healthy adults. Brown 2022 (full text) notes prior light exposure modulates later sensitivity to light and that these effects 'are certainly not limited to earlier parts of the day', suggesting benefit from high light throughout the day, while recommending <=10 lux melanopic EDI in the 3 hours before habitual sleep.

citation.title: Recommendations for daytime, evening, and nighttime indoor light exposure to best support physiology, sleep, and wakefulness in healthy adults.

items.plain: Your body is coldest a couple of hours before you usually wake.
items.paragraph: The coldest point of your body's daily temperature cycle. In this model it falls about 2 hours before you usually wake up, so about 5 a.m. if you wake at 7. Bright light, exercise, or caffeine in the 2 to 4 hours before it nudges your body clock later; the same things in the hours just after it nudge your clock earlier. Some people use the timing to shift their clock before travel.
items.category: Physiological and Biological Factors Affecting Sleep
items.subcategory: Light Exposure and Circadian Rhythm Regulation

items.plain: Breathe in for 4, hold for 4, out for 4, hold for 4, and repeat.
items.paragraph: A counted breathing pattern: breathe in for 4, hold for 4, breathe out for 4, hold for 4, then repeat. Picturing the numbers as you count gives your mind something to focus on. Beginners can start with 4 to 5 rounds.
items.category: Physiological and Biological Factors Affecting Sleep

findings.keyResult: Box breathing was one of three breathwork arms; the abstract reports the clearest benefit for cyclic sighing, with breathwork overall improving mood and reducing respiratory rate more than mindfulness meditation.

citation.authors: Balban MY, Neri E, Kogon MM, et al.
citation.title: Brief structured respiration practices enhance mood and reduce physiological arousal.

items.plain: Breathe in fully through your nose, then breathe out slowly and completely.
items.paragraph: A breathing pattern for calming down fast: breathe in through the nose until your lungs feel full, then, without holding, let the air out slowly and completely. A few rounds is often enough to quiet racing thoughts.
items.category: Physiological and Biological Factors Affecting Sleep

findings.keyResult: Remote RCT of three daily 5-min breathwork exercises (cyclic sighing, box breathing, cyclic hyperventilation with retention) vs mindfulness meditation for 1 month. Breathwork, especially exhale-focused cyclic sighing, produced greater improvement in mood (p < 0.05) and reduction in respiratory rate (p < 0.05) than mindfulness meditation.

citation.authors: Balban MY, Neri E, Kogon MM, et al.
citation.title: Brief structured respiration practices enhance mood and reduce physiological arousal.

items.plain: Breathe slowly so your belly, not your chest, rises and falls.
items.paragraph: Breathing deeply so your belly rises as you breathe in and falls as you breathe out, slowly and through the nose. It is the base skill for most other relaxation breathing exercises.
items.category: Physiological and Biological Factors Affecting Sleep

items.plain: Breathe in through one nostril and out the other, switching sides.
items.paragraph: A breathing exercise where you close one nostril with a finger, breathe in through the other, then switch sides for the breath out and the next breath in. Beginners can try 5 to 10 rounds. It is used to settle strong emotions.
items.category: Physiological and Biological Factors Affecting Sleep

items.plain: Lying still with your eyes closed rests you a little, but it is not a substitute for sleep.
items.plainBefore: If you can't sleep, lying still with your eyes closed still rests your body.
items.paragraph: Lying still in the dark and quiet, awake, with your eyes closed. It is not sleep, but it can still rest the body, which can take pressure off the effort to fall asleep.
items.category: Psychological and Emotional Factors Affecting Sleep

findings.keyResult: Sleep Health Foundation: 'Rest is good – it does not have to be sleep. Don't label yourself as an insomniac as this will increase your worry and frustration.' (Same page advises getting up after 20-30 minutes awake.)

citation.title: Sleep Hygiene: Good Sleep Habits (fact sheet)

findings.population: good sleepers (n=150) vs people with insomnia (n=173), China
findings.keyResult: Cross-sectional survey. Staying in bed while awake during the night and in the morning differed between good sleepers and people with insomnia (Cohen's d 1.33 and 0.85) and correlated with insomnia severity; bedtime, rising time and total time in bed did not differ (d <0.01, 0.07, 0.07). Authors note staying in bed awake 'could be only signs of insomnia symptoms'.

citation.authors: Birling Y, Li G, Jia M, et al.
citation.title: Is insomnia disorder associated with time in bed extension?

findings.keyResult: 'Lying in bed with your eyes closed is almost as good as sleeping' rated a myth: falseness M 4.63 (SD 0.74), public health significance M 3.86 (SD 1.07).

citation.authors: Robbins R, Grandner MA, Buxton OM, et al.
citation.title: Sleep myths: an expert-led study to identify false beliefs about sleep that impinge upon population sleep health practices.

items.plain: Use the last hour before bed for chores, then washing up, then something calm.
items.paragraph: A set hour before bed split into three 20-minute parts: one for chores and last-minute tasks, one for hygiene such as brushing teeth, washing your face, or a warm shower, and one for something slow and calming such as reading, meditation, or prayer. Setting an alarm an hour before bedtime reminds you to start.
items.category: Sleep Hygiene (General Behavioral and Environmental Factors)

items.plain: Stop alcohol 3 hours, food 2 hours and drinks 1 hour before bed.
items.paragraph: A countdown before bed: stop alcohol 3 hours before, stop eating 2 hours before, and stop drinking fluids 1 hour before. People who need fluids for medicine, diabetes, or constant thirst should skip the fluid cutoff and ask their doctor.
items.category: Physiological and Biological Factors Affecting Sleep
items.audienceNote: Skip the fluid step if you need fluids for medicine, diabetes or thirst.

items.plain: On hot nights, a frozen water bottle wrapped in a sock can cool you down in bed.
items.paragraph: A low-tech way to cool your body before sleep: freeze a bottle of water, put it in a sock, and place one by each hip in bed.
items.category: Sleep Hygiene (General Behavioral and Environmental Factors)

findings.keyResult: With very low to low certainty, cooling bedding strategies (mattress, topper, pillow) showed no differences vs control in sleep onset latency, sleep efficiency, sleep stages, wake after sleep onset or total sleep time, although some studies showed acute lowering of core body temperature (p < 0.05).

citation.title: Does body cooling facilitated by bedding compared to control condition improve sleep among adults (18-64 years old)? A systematic review and meta-analysis.

items.plain: Some advise waiting 90 minutes or more after waking for your first coffee.
items.paragraph: Drink water first and wait about 90 minutes after waking before your first cup of coffee.
items.category: Physiological and Biological Factors Affecting Sleep

positions.says: About 90 minutes, because cortisol drops by then (unverified).
90-120 minutes, to spread energy and want less caffeine later.

items.plain: Pick a time in the early afternoon after which you have no caffeine.
items.paragraph: Pick a time in the early afternoon after which you stop caffeine, so it has worn off by bedtime. Caffeine can stay in your body for many hours.
items.category: Physiological and Biological Factors Affecting Sleep

findings.keyResult: Guidance differs by body: NHS insomnia page: 'do not smoke or drink alcohol, tea or coffee at least 6 hours before going to bed'. NHLBI: avoid nicotine and caffeine; 'The effects of caffeine can last up to 8 hours.' CDC and AASM patient pages: avoid caffeine 'in the afternoon or evening'. Sleep Health Foundation: 'Some say caffeine should be avoided for at least 3 to 7 hours before going to sleep. Others say no caffeine after lunch time if you have sleep problems.'
findings.whatWasRead: guideline page (NHS, NHLBI, CDC, AASM sleepeducation.org, SHF pages all read)

citation.title: Insomnia (page last reviewed 19 March 2024)

findings.keyResult: Narrative review: caffeine plasma levels peak about 30 minutes after oral intake and a single dose has a half-life of 3-7 hours; in a study of 12 healthy young adults, 400 mg of caffeine taken up to 6 hours before bedtime disturbed both subjective and objective sleep. Overall, epidemiologic and experimental research generally supported links between individual sleep hygiene recommendations and sleep, but direct effects in the general population remain largely untested.

citation.title: The role of sleep hygiene in promoting public health: A review of empirical evidence

findings.keyResult: Caffeine reduced total sleep time by 45 min and sleep efficiency by 7%, increased sleep onset latency by 9 min and wake after sleep onset by 12 min, and reduced deep sleep (N3/N4) by 11.4 min (-1.4%). To avoid reductions in total sleep time, coffee (107 mg per 250 mL) should be consumed at least 8.8 h before bedtime, and a standard pre-workout supplement (217.5 mg) at least 13.2 h before bedtime.

citation.title: The effect of caffeine on subsequent sleep: A systematic review and meta-analysis.

findings.keyResult: 400 mg caffeine taken at bedtime, 3 h before, or 6 h before bedtime each significantly disturbed sleep compared with placebo (p < 0.05 for all). The authors conclude caffeine 6 h before bed has important disruptive effects and support refraining from substantial caffeine for a minimum of 6 hours before bedtime.

citation.title: Caffeine effects on sleep taken 0, 3, or 6 hours before going to bed.

items.plain: If you're naturally a night owl or early bird, set your bedtime with that in mind.
items.paragraph: Your chronotype is your natural lean toward mornings or evenings. Going to bed much earlier or later than your body prefers can make falling asleep harder, so set your bedtime with your own pattern in mind.
items.category: Sleep Hygiene (General Behavioral and Environmental Factors)

findings.keyResult: Practical intervention (earlier wake/sleep times for light exposure, fixed meal times, caffeine timing, exercise) produced a significant advance of ~2 h in sleep/wake timing and circadian markers with no adverse effect on sleep duration, plus improvements in self-reported depression and stress and in morning reaction time and grip strength.

citation.title: Resetting the late timing of 'night owls' has a positive impact on mental health and performance.

items.plain: One expert says to stay in bed and breathe slowly when you wake at night.
items.paragraph: When you wake in the middle of the night, stay in bed with the lights off and use slow breathing to settle, instead of getting up, walking around, or picking up your phone. If you do not need the bathroom, skip the trip. Keep a glass of room-temperature water by the bed.
items.category: Psychological and Emotional Factors Affecting Sleep

findings.keyResult: 34 participants given countercontrol behavioural therapy (22 immediate, 12 delayed). Countercontrol reduced the sleep complaint for the total group by about 30% at the end of treatment, with gradual improvement continuing through a 4-week follow-up; older people benefited as much as younger.

citation.authors: Davies R, Lacks P, Storandt M, et al.
citation.title: Countercontrol treatment of sleep-maintenance insomnia in relation to age.

items.plain: Stop work or schoolwork at least an hour before bed.
items.paragraph: Deadlines push us to sacrifice rest, but the late-night work rarely pays off the next day. Finishing earlier allows the brain to settle and restores clarity for tomorrow.
items.category: Psychological and Emotional Factors Affecting Sleep

items.plain: Plan get-togethers earlier in the day so late nights are the exception.
items.paragraph: Connection is vital, but it doesn’t need to cost tomorrow’s energy. By shifting when and how we socialize, we keep both joy and rest intact.
items.category: Sleep Hygiene (General Behavioral and Environmental Factors)

items.plain: Stretch or move your body soon after you wake up.
items.category: Physiological and Biological Factors Affecting Sleep

items.plain: Use an alarm clock instead of your phone, so the phone can stay out of the bedroom.
items.category: Sleep Hygiene (General Behavioral and Environmental Factors)

items.plain: If poor sleep lasts more than a few weeks, talk with a health professional.
items.paragraph: Anxiety and depression can complicate sleep, but simple practices and self-compassion change the tone of nights.
items.category: Medical and Pharmacological Considerations

positions.says: If poor sleep persists for more than a few weeks.
If changes to sleep habits have not helped and you've had trouble sleeping for months (per the guidelines search).

findings.keyResult: NHS: see a GP if changing sleeping habits has not helped, if you've had trouble sleeping for months, or if insomnia makes daily life hard to manage. Short-term insomnia is under 3 months; long-term is 3 months or longer. Treatments: CBT face-to-face or via online self-help; sleeping pills rarely prescribed and only for a few days or weeks at most; pharmacy sleep aids may help for 1 to 2 weeks and shouldn't be taken longer.

citation.title: Insomnia (page last reviewed 19 March 2024)

items.plain: After a bad night, go easy on yourself; one rough night is feedback, not failure.
items.category: Psychological and Emotional Factors Affecting Sleep

findings.keyResult: Medium correlation between self-compassion and subjective sleep quality, r = 0.303 (95% CI 0.244 to 0.360). In three experimental studies, small increase in self-reported sleep quality vs control, Hedges' g = 0.484 (0.148 to 0.821).

citation.title: The Relationship between Self-Compassion and Sleep Quality: An Overview of a Seven-Year German Research Program.

findings.keyResult: Self-compassion associated with physical health (r = .18) and health behaviour (r = .26); among the strongest effects was sleep. Multi-session self-compassion interventions predicted better health and health behaviour; single-session inductions did not.

citation.title: Self-compassion, physical health, and health behaviour: a meta-analysis.

items.plain: If you use cannabis, keep it away from bedtime and notice how it affects your sleep.
items.paragraph: Cannabis affects sleep differently for everyone, but heavy use often suppresses restorative REM cycles. Reflection and moderation bring clarity.
items.category: Physiological and Biological Factors Affecting Sleep
items.audienceNote: Legal status differs by country and state.

findings.keyResult: Compared with placebo, medical cannabis may have little to no clinically meaningful effect on sleep quality/satisfaction (SMD -0.49, 95%CI -1.06 to 0.08; very low certainty), total sleep time (MD 7.68 minutes, 95% CI -23.04 to 38.39; very low certainty) or daytime functioning, and may result in a slight increase in adverse events (OR 11.25, 95% CI 4.46 to 28.35; low certainty).

citation.title: Medical cannabis for the treatment of insomnia.

findings.keyResult: Cannabis administration did not consistently alter sleep duration, latency, wake time, efficiency or staging. Early reports of reduced REM came from small, high-THC studies; newer studies show mixed and often no REM suppression. Withdrawal from regular use was consistently associated with disturbed sleep: less total sleep, longer sleep onset latency and REM rebound.

citation.title: Cannabis and sleep architecture: A systematic review and meta-analysis.

findings.keyResult: Sleep improved in 7 of 19 randomized studies and 7 of 12 uncontrolled trials. No significant differences between THC and CBD. Benefits mostly in pain-related conditions; no significant effects in healthy participants. Subjective improvements were common but objective sleep architecture did not improve. Adverse events (headache, sedation, dizziness) were more frequent at higher doses.

citation.title: Cannabis dosing and administration for sleep: a systematic review.

findings.keyResult: Cannabis use within 3 hours of sleep was associated with more wake after sleep onset (median 60.5 vs 45.8 minutes; rate ratio 1.59) and a higher proportion of stage 1 sleep (median 15.2% vs 12.3%). Frequent users (>20 days per month) also had more wake, longer REM latency and lower sleep efficiency. No association with longer or more efficient sleep.

citation.title: The impact of cannabis use proximal to sleep and cannabinoid metabolites on sleep architecture.

findings.keyResult: AASM position: medical cannabis and/or its synthetic extracts should not be used to treat OSA because of unreliable delivery methods and insufficient evidence of effectiveness, tolerability and safety; patients should discuss treatment options with a licensed provider at an accredited sleep facility.

citation.title: Medical Cannabis and the Treatment of Obstructive Sleep Apnea: An American Academy of Sleep Medicine Position Statement.

items.plain: Get plenty of bright light during the day, and keep your nights dark.
items.category: Physiological and Biological Factors Affecting Sleep
items.subcategory: Light Exposure and Circadian Rhythm Regulation

findings.population: UK Biobank adults wearing light sensors for 1 week (N=88,905), mean age 62.4
findings.keyResult: Brighter day light was associated with incrementally lower all-cause mortality (aHR 0.84 to 0.90 at 50-70th percentiles, 0.74 to 0.84 at 70-90th, 0.66 to 0.83 at 90-100th) and brighter night light with incrementally higher mortality (aHR 1.15 to 1.18 at 70-90th, 1.21 to 1.34 at 90-100th), compared with the 0-50th percentiles.

citation.title: Brighter nights and darker days predict higher mortality risk: A prospective analysis of personal light exposure in >88,000 individuals.
citation.journal: Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A

items.plain: Sleep tips alone rarely fix long-lasting insomnia; if poor sleep goes on for months, ask about CBT-I.
items.category: Medical and Pharmacological Considerations

findings.keyResult: AASM 2021: 'We suggest that clinicians not use sleep hygiene as a single-component therapy for the treatment of chronic insomnia disorder in adults. (CONDITIONAL).' Only 3 RCTs compared sleep hygiene to wait-list, minimal interventions or placebo; resources for sleep hygiene alone 'may divert resources and delay the use of other single- or multicomponent behavioral interventions that are more effective.' Sleep hygiene defined as general recommendations about lifestyle (diet, exercise, substance use) and environment (light, noise, temperature).

citation.authors: Edinger JD, Arnedt JT, Bertisch SM, et al.
citation.title: Behavioral and psychological treatments for chronic insomnia disorder in adults: an American Academy of Sleep Medicine clinical practice guideline

findings.population: adults with poor sleep or insomnia
findings.keyResult: 15 studies (12 vs CBT-I, 3 vs mindfulness; none vs sham/no treatment): significant pre-post improvements after sleep hygiene education with small to medium effect size; SHE significantly less efficacious than CBT-I (medium to large difference). Pre-post improvement and SHE-CBT-I difference averaged 5% and 8% in diary sleep efficiency, and two points on the PSQI; only subjective measures were significant.

citation.title: Sleep hygiene education as a treatment of insomnia: a systematic review and meta-analysis

findings.keyResult: 42 RCTs: significant pre-post improvement in ISI (MD = 3.4, 95% CI [2.08, 4.64]), but SHE was inferior to CBT-I (MD = 3.8, 95% CI [2.92, 4.76]), partial CBT-I (MD = 4.5, 95% CI [3.33, 5.60]), exercises (MD = 2.9, 95% CI [0.81, 5.04]) and acupressure (MD = 1.9, 95% CI [0.82, 3.00]). 85.71% of trials had high overall risk of bias.

citation.title: Effects of sleep hygiene education for insomnia: A systematic review and meta-analysis

items.plain: Don't try to split your sleep into several short blocks a day to need less sleep.
items.category: Sleep Hygiene (General Behavioral and Environmental Factors)

findings.keyResult: NSF panel reviewed 22 relevant papers (from 40,672 screened) and found no evidence supporting benefits from polyphasic sleep schedules (excluding naps/siestas); they are associated with adverse physical health, mental health and performance outcomes. 'Striving to adopt a schedule that significantly reduces the amount of sleep per 24 hours and/or fragments sleep into multiple episodes throughout the 24-hour day is not recommended.'

citation.title: Adverse impact of polyphasic sleep patterns in humans: Report of the National Sleep Foundation sleep timing and variability consensus panel

items.plain: Teens' body clocks run later; support later school start times instead of blaming teens for sleeping late.
items.category: Sleep Hygiene (General Behavioral and Environmental Factors)

findings.keyResult: NSF Adolescent Sleep Health Conference (22 experts): recommendations include implementing healthy school start times and adopting permanent standard time, raising awareness of sleep's impact on work and driving, and prioritizing sleep health equity; adolescents should be included as contributors.

citation.authors: Dautovich ND, Gunn HE, Dzierzewski JM, et al.
citation.title: Adolescent sleep health: Recommendations from the National Sleep Foundation

findings.keyResult: 'If school starts later, adolescents will stay up that much later' was endorsed by 69% of parents/caregivers; experts rated falseness M 4.1 (SD 0.9), public health significance M 4.6 (SD 0.7). Experts also rated 'If adolescents can't get up for school, they are lazy' (4.4) and 'An adolescent's sleep schedule is largely out of their control' (4.3) as false.

citation.authors: Robbins R, Beebe DW, Byars KC, et al.
citation.title: Adolescent sleep myths: Identifying false beliefs that impact adolescent sleep and well-being.

findings.keyResult: 11 unique studies with 297,994 participants. Quality of evidence very low. Six studies reported significant positive relationships between later school start times and amount of sleep; academic outcomes, absenteeism and alertness were mixed. Authors could not determine effects with any confidence.

citation.authors: Marx R, Tanner-Smith EE, Davison CM, et al.
citation.title: Later school start times for supporting the education, health, and well-being of high school students.

findings.keyResult: Six studies included. Delayed school start time was associated with an average increase in sleep duration of 69 min (SMD 0.63, moderate effect); depressive symptoms (five studies) pooled SMD -0.20 (small). High heterogeneity in both analyses.

citation.authors: Wang RC, Lee MI, Aroul GS, et al.
citation.title: Delayed school start times to improve sleep duration and mitigate depression in adolescents: a systematic review and meta-analysis.

items.plain: Put babies to sleep on their backs, on a firm flat surface, in your room but not in your bed.
items.category: Sleep Hygiene (General Behavioral and Environmental Factors)

findings.keyResult: AAP 2022: safe sleep environment includes supine positioning; a firm, noninclined sleep surface; room sharing without bed sharing; avoidance of soft bedding and overheating. Additional SIDS risk reduction: human milk feeding; avoiding exposure to nicotine, alcohol, marijuana, opioids and illicit drugs; routine immunization; and pacifier use. About 3500 US infants die of sleep-related deaths each year.

citation.title: Sleep-Related Infant Deaths: Updated 2022 Recommendations for Reducing Infant Deaths in the Sleep Environment

findings.keyResult: AAP policy: about 3500 US infants die of sleep-related deaths each year. Recommends supine positioning; a firm, noninclined sleep surface; room sharing without bed sharing; avoiding soft bedding and overheating; plus human milk feeding, avoiding nicotine, alcohol, marijuana, opioids and illicit drugs, routine immunization and pacifier use.

citation.authors: Moon RY, Carlin RF, Hand I, et al.
citation.title: Sleep-Related Infant Deaths: Updated 2022 Recommendations for Reducing Infant Deaths in the Sleep Environment.

findings.keyResult: Eleven studies. Combined OR for SIDS in all bed-sharing versus non-bed-sharing infants 2.89 (95% CI 1.99-4.18). Highest risk for infants of smoking mothers (OR 6.27; 95% CI 3.94-9.99) and infants <12 weeks old (OR 10.37; 95% CI 4.44-24.21).

citation.authors: Vennemann MM, Hense HW, Bajanowski T, et al.
citation.title: Bed sharing and the risk of sudden infant death syndrome: can we resolve the debate?

items.plain: If trying hard to fall asleep keeps you awake, stop trying and let sleep come on its own.
items.category: Psychological and Emotional Factors Affecting Sleep

findings.keyResult: 10 trials. Compared with passive comparators, paradoxical intention led to large improvements in key insomnia symptoms and great reductions in sleep-related performance anxiety; relative to active comparators improvements were smaller but still moderate for several outcomes.

citation.authors: Jansson-Fröjmark M, Alfonsson S, Bohman B, et al.
citation.title: Paradoxical intention for insomnia: A systematic review and meta-analysis.

findings.keyResult: Proposes the attention-intention-effort pathway: sleep is a relatively automatic process that can be inhibited by focused attention on sleep and by direct attempts to control it.

citation.authors: Espie CA, Broomfield NM, MacMahon KM, et al.
citation.title: The attention-intention-effort pathway in the development of psychophysiologic insomnia: a theoretical review.

findings.keyResult: ACT vs waitlist/standard control: insomnia severity SMD -0.67 (95% CI -1.08 to -0.25). No significant difference vs CBT-I at post-treatment (SMD 0.21, -0.02 to 0.43) or 6 months (SMD 0.14, -0.15 to 0.42); CBT-I gave higher remission at post-treatment (RR 0.81, 0.67 to 0.98). Authors: CBT-I remains the gold standard.

citation.authors: Barroso D, de Paula Portilho N, Garbacka-Struzik A, et al.
citation.title: Acceptance and commitment therapy for insomnia: an updated meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.

findings.keyResult: Compared with passive comparators, paradoxical intention led to large improvements in key insomnia symptoms and large reductions in sleep-related performance anxiety; versus active comparators the improvements were smaller but still moderate for several central outcomes. Methodologically stronger studies are needed.

citation.authors: Jansson-Fröjmark M, Alfonsson S, Bohman B, et al.
citation.title: Paradoxical intention for insomnia: A systematic review and meta-analysis.

items.plain: Listening to calm music for 25 to 60 minutes at bedtime may help you sleep better.
items.category: Psychological and Emotional Factors Affecting Sleep

findings.population: adults with insomnia symptoms (13 RCTs, 1007 participants)
findings.keyResult: Cochrane: moderate-certainty evidence that music improved PSQI sleep quality vs no treatment/usual care (MD -2.79, 95% CI -3.86 to -1.72; 10 studies, 708 participants). Low-certainty evidence for shorter sleep onset latency, longer total sleep time and better efficiency (subjective); objective measures in 3 studies showed no improvement. No adverse events reported.

citation.authors: Jespersen KV, Pando-Naude V, Koenig J, et al.
citation.title: Listening to music for insomnia in adults.

items.plain: Falling asleep anywhere, any time is a sign you're short on sleep, not a sign of good sleep.
items.category: Busting sleep myths

findings.keyResult: 'Being able to fall asleep "anytime, anywhere" is a sign of a healthy sleep system' rated a myth: falseness M 4.75 (SD 0.46), public health significance M 4.00 (SD 0.93).

citation.authors: Robbins R, Grandner MA, Buxton OM, et al.
citation.title: Sleep myths: an expert-led study to identify false beliefs about sleep that impinge upon population sleep health practices.

items.plain: Hitting snooze for a short while is fine for most people.
items.category: Busting sleep myths

findings.keyResult: Experts classified 'Hitting the snooze when you wake up is better than getting up when the alarm first goes off' as a myth: falseness M 3.75 (SD 1.04), public health significance M 2.75 (SD 1.04).

citation.authors: Robbins R, Grandner MA, Buxton OM, et al.
citation.title: Sleep myths: an expert-led study to identify false beliefs about sleep that impinge upon population sleep health practices.

findings.population: habitual snoozers, adults (lab study n = 31; survey n = 1732)
findings.keyResult: Survey of 1732 respondents: snoozing is widespread, especially in younger people and later chronotypes. In a within-subject lab study of 31 habitual snoozers, 30 min of snoozing improved or did not affect cognitive test performance on rising versus abrupt awakening; snoozing cost about 6 min of sleep and prevented awakenings from slow-wave sleep (N3); no clear effects on cortisol awakening response, morning sleepiness, mood, or overnight sleep architecture.

citation.authors: Sundelin T, Landry S, Axelsson J
citation.title: Is snoozing losing? Why intermittent morning alarms are used and how they affect sleep, cognition, cortisol, and mood.

items.plain: Melatonin isn't automatically safe for children and teens just because it's natural; ask a clinician first.
items.category: Medical and Pharmacological Considerations

findings.keyResult: 'Melatonin supplements are safe for adolescents because they are natural' was endorsed by 66% of parents/caregivers; experts rated falseness M 4.0 (SD 0.7), public health significance M 4.0 (SD 0.9).

citation.authors: Robbins R, Beebe DW, Byars KC, et al.
citation.title: Adolescent sleep myths: Identifying false beliefs that impact adolescent sleep and well-being.

items.plain: From about 28 weeks of pregnancy, go to sleep on your side (left or right), not on your back.
items.category: Medical and Pharmacological Considerations

findings.keyResult: IPD meta-analysis of case-control studies (cases n = 851; controls n = 2257). Supine going-to-sleep position associated with increased odds of late stillbirth (aOR 2.63, 95% CI 1.72-4.04) compared with left side. Right side had similar odds to left (aOR 1.04, 95% CI 0.83-1.31). Population attributable risk for supine going-to-sleep position 5.8% (3.2-9.2).

citation.authors: Cronin RS, Li M, Thompson JMD, et al.
citation.title: An Individual Participant Data Meta-analysis of Maternal Going-to-Sleep Position, Interactions with Fetal Vulnerability, and the Risk of Late Stillbirth.

findings.keyResult: No association between non-left lateral or supine sleep at the first visit (aOR 1.00 [95% CI 0.89-1.14]) or third visit (aOR 0.99 [95% CI 0.89-1.11]) and the composite of stillbirth, small-for-gestational-age or gestational hypertensive disorders. Objectively measured supine sleep >=50% of the time was not linked to the composite outcome.

citation.authors: Silver RM, Hunter S, Reddy UM, et al.
citation.title: Prospective Evaluation of Maternal Sleep Position Through 30 Weeks of Gestation and Adverse Pregnancy Outcomes.

items.plain: For older adults, sleeping pills usually help only a little and raise the risk of falls and confusion; try other approaches first.
items.category: Medical and Pharmacological Considerations

findings.keyResult: 24 RCTs (2417 participants). With sedatives: sleep quality improved (effect size 0.14), total sleep time increased (mean 25.2 minutes), night awakenings decreased (0.63). Adverse cognitive events 4.78 times more common (95% CI 1.47 to 15.47), adverse psychomotor events 2.61 times more common (1.12 to 6.09), daytime fatigue 3.82 times more common (1.88 to 7.80) than placebo.

items.plain: Alcohol may make you drowsy, but it makes sleep worse later in the night.
items.paragraph: While alcohol may induce drowsiness and help you fall asleep faster, it negatively impacts the quality of your rest[77][78].
items.category: Busting sleep myths
items.evidenceSummary:
- #### Truth: While alcohol may induce drowsiness and help you fall asleep faster, it negatively impacts the quality of your rest[77][78].

Alcohol disrupts the normal sleep cycle by reducing REM (rapid eye movement) sleep, which is essential for cognitive function, memory consolidation, and emotional regulation. As the body metabolizes alcohol, sleep becomes more fragmented, leading to frequent awakenings throughout the night. This results in grogginess, reduced alertness, and impaired performance the next day, despite feeling initially sleepy after drinking.

Additionally, alcohol can contribute to sleep disorders such as insomnia and sleep apnea[79][80]. It relaxes the muscles in the throat, increasing the likelihood of airway obstruction, which can lead to snoring or more severe breathing interruptions. Over time, relying on alcohol as a sleep aid can lead to dependency, further worsening sleep problems[78][81]. Instead of using alcohol to wind down, healthier alternatives such as reading, meditation, or maintaining a consistent bedtime routine can promote better sleep quality without negative side effects.

items.plain: Sleeping in on weekends doesn't fully make up for short sleep during the week.
items.paragraph: Sleeping in on weekends may provide temporary relief from sleep deprivation, but it does not fully restore the negative effects of lost sleep[82][83].
items.category: Busting sleep myths
items.evidenceSummary:
- #### Truth: Sleeping in on weekends may provide temporary relief from sleep deprivation, but it does not fully restore the negative effects of lost sleep[82][83].

Chronic sleep debt affects cognitive function, mood, metabolism, and overall health, and trying to compensate with extra sleep on weekends can create an irregular sleep pattern. This inconsistency can disrupt the body's circadian rhythm, making it harder to fall asleep and wake up at regular times during the week. Studies show that even after catching up on sleep, individuals may still experience impaired alertness, reduced reaction time, and difficulty concentrating.

Moreover, relying on weekend sleep-ins can contribute to a cycle of poor sleep habits. Late wake-up times on weekends often lead to staying up later at night, making it even harder to return to an early bedtime when the workweek begins[84]. This phenomenon, sometimes referred to as "social jet lag," can have long-term consequences on health, including an increased risk of obesity, diabetes, and cardiovascular disease. Instead of trying to make up for lost sleep on weekends, maintaining a consistent sleep schedule—going to bed and waking up at the same time every day—is a more effective strategy for overall sleep health.

items.plain: Regular exercise helps sleep, but hard workouts right before bed can keep you up.
items.paragraph: Regular exercise is well known for promoting better sleep by reducing stress, improving mood, and regulating the body's circadian rhythm[17]. However, engaging in intense workouts too close to bedtime can have the opposite effect.
items.category: Busting sleep myths
items.evidenceSummary:
- #### Truth: Regular exercise is well known for promoting better sleep by reducing stress, improving mood, and regulating the body's circadian rhythm[17]. However, engaging in intense workouts too close to bedtime can have the opposite effect.

High-intensity exercise raises heart rate, core body temperature, and adrenaline levels, which can make it harder to relax and fall asleep[85]. The body's natural cooling process, which signals the brain that it's time to rest, can be delayed when exercise is performed late at night, leading to difficulties in sleep onset and reduced sleep quality.

To maximize the sleep benefits of exercise, it is best to finish vigorous workouts at least three hours before bedtime[86][87]. This allows the body enough time to cool down and shift into a more relaxed state conducive to sleep. Lighter forms of physical activity, such as yoga or stretching, can be beneficial before bed, as they promote relaxation without overstimulating the nervous system. Establishing a consistent exercise routine earlier in the day can enhance overall sleep quality and ensure a smoother transition into restful sleep at night.

items.plain: Falling asleep to TV can make sleep lighter and more broken.
items.paragraph: Many people believe that watching TV before bed helps them unwind and fall asleep, but it can actually do more harm than good[88].
items.category: Busting sleep myths
items.evidenceSummary:
- #### Truth: Many people believe that watching TV before bed helps them unwind and fall asleep, but it can actually do more harm than good[88].

The blue light emitted by screens interferes with the body’s natural production of melatonin, the hormone responsible for regulating sleep. When melatonin levels are suppressed, it becomes harder to feel sleepy, leading to delayed sleep onset and reduced sleep quality[18][19]. Even if someone manages to fall asleep with the TV on, the stimulating content—whether it’s an engaging show, fast-paced action, or loud sounds—can keep the brain active, making sleep more fragmented and less restorative.

A better alternative is to establish a relaxing, screen-free bedtime routine. Engaging in activities such as reading a book, practicing mindfulness, or listening to calming music can help signal the body that it's time to rest[76]. Dimming the lights and reducing exposure to screens at least an hour before bed allows melatonin levels to rise naturally, leading to easier sleep initiation and deeper, more restorative rest. Creating a consistent nighttime routine without screen distractions can improve overall sleep quality and help maintain a healthy sleep-wake cycle.

items.plain: Loud, frequent snoring can be a sign of sleep apnea and is worth checking.
items.paragraph: Occasional snoring is common and may result from factors like nasal congestion, sleep position, or fatigue[89][90]. However, frequent and loud snoring can be a warning sign of obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), a serious sleep disorder in which breathing repeatedly stops and starts during sleep[91].
items.category: Busting sleep myths
items.evidenceSummary:
OSA occurs when the muscles in the throat relax excessively, causing a temporary blockage of the airway. These pauses in breathing can lead to sudden drops in oxygen levels, triggering the brain to wake the person momentarily—often without them realizing it. This repeated disruption prevents deep, restorative sleep, leading to daytime fatigue, difficulty concentrating, and increased irritability.

Left untreated, sleep apnea can have significant long-term health consequences. The repeated oxygen deprivation and sleep fragmentation put extra strain on the cardiovascular system, increasing the risk of high blood pressure, heart disease, stroke, and type 2 diabetes[92][93]. Additionally, untreated sleep apnea has been linked to weight gain, weakened immune function, and a higher likelihood of accidents due to excessive daytime sleepiness[94]. If snoring is loud, persistent, or accompanied by gasping, choking, or pauses in breathing, it is essential to seek medical evaluation. Lifestyle changes, such as maintaining a healthy weight, adjusting sleep position, or using a CPAP (continuous positive airway pressure) machine, can help manage sleep apnea and improve overall health.[95][96]
